IMHO the first one was the better of the two. It's not perfect (Xen anyone?) but it feels like more of a unified game. Half-Life 2 was developed using a "hub" system where different teams which almost never communicated worked on the different set pieces of the game. Then it was all put together at the end. This shows, and shows badly. There is little thematic, gameplay, or story connection between the areas you visit. I mean, they give you a weak pretense as to why the story needs to move to the next set piece. But it's pretty meh.

On top of that, the game is full of rather gimmicky physics "puzzles" that almost exclusively involve placing something heavy on a lever and/or pulley system. Make sure you "ooo" and "ahh" appropriately. And notice that most games have gone back to just doing buttons, and saving the physics engines for explosions and driving.

Also, I always felt the actual FPS gameplay of HL2 was severely diminished from HL1. Fewer weapons, fewer enemy types, worse AI.

Not to mention all the technical problems when the game launched. For years I had sound stuttering across 3 different rigs I built. Plus the game ran extremely poorly on Geforce 5000 series cards on account of how the shaders were written almost exclusively for ATI 24-bit shader units. Geforce cards only did 16-bit and 32-bit, and it's 32-bit performed half as the 16-bit performance. Enterprising hackers just replaced all the 24-bit shaders (which defaulted to 32-bit on Geforce cards) with 16-bit shaders and the game immediately sprang to life on Geforce 5000 series cards.

Admittedly, the Geforce 5000 series was a serious misstep by Nvidia.

Despite all that, I've probably played through Half-Life 2 a half dozen times.
